title: Embattled Serbian president resigns, paving way for early elections
description: Serbia's president has resigned after more than a year of student-led protests and growing public discontent over allegations of government corruption
body: Serbia's president has resigned after more than a year of student-led protests and growing public discontent over allegations of government corruption.Aleksandar Vučić said his administration had preserved peace and stability during his nine-year tenure as he addressed supporters outside the presidential building in the capital, Belgrade.He had already announced his intention to resign in June and is currently standing to be his party's candidate for prime minister in the upcoming parliamentary elections. Vučić cannot run for a third presidential term under Serbia's constitution.The pro-Russian populist's administration has been dogged by anger over alleged corner-cutting.It was the collapse of the Novi Sad railway station's roof, killing 16 people, that first galvanised anger towards the government in 2024.Protests involving a wide range of citizens - from students and teachers to workers and farmers - followed.Demonstrators believed that the disaster reflected more than a decade of governing by the Progressive Party of Vucic, who closely associated himself with the station's renovation, which was supposed to be a symbol of Serbia's progress.A series of resignations of those under the embattled president failed to placate the protesters, who continued to demonstrate throughout this summer, turning to unrest following accusations of police brutality.Vučić's presidency was due to expire next year. Under Serbia's constitution, presidential elections must be held no more than three months after his resignation.This means Serbians will go to the polls twice before the end of the year.Vučić said the presidential election will take place more than a month after the snap parliamentary election in late October, itself called in response to the protests, which had added calls for a vote to their list of demands.He had earlier announced that he planned to run in that election as Progressive Party's leader, leaving the possibility he could retain a position at the top of Serbian politics.Parliamentary speaker Ana Brnabić, also a Progressive Party member, will assume the role of interim president until a new one is elected.Vučić used his constitutional powers to pardon 49 people, including 23 students and party loyalists suspected of offences related to what he called the "terrible events we have gone through over the past year and a half", according to Serbian public broadcaster RTS.The upcoming parliamentary elections will pit Vučić's Progressive Party against a student-led, anti-corruption movement called Students Win and a coalition of pro-Western opposition parties known as European Serbia.Vucic has been a fixture of Serbian politics for more than a decade, becoming prime minister in 2014, before being elected to his first term as president in 2017.He has publicly said he wants Serbia to join the EU while courting close ties with Russia and opening Serbia up to Chinese investment.

schema.headline: Embattled Serbian president resigns, paving way for early elections

title: One dead as nor'easter storm pummels New York and New Jersey
description: Figure caption, Watch: Huge waves pummel northeast US as storm barrels throughByKwasi Gyamfi AsieduUpdated 3 hours agoTens of millions of people acros
body: Figure caption, Watch: Huge waves pummel northeast US as storm barrels throughByKwasi Gyamfi AsieduUpdated 3 hours agoTens of millions of people across the north-eastern US have found themselves in the path of a powerful weekend storm bringing coastal flooding, power cuts, travel chaos and cancelled stadium events.The so-called nor'easter brought "dangerous coastal flooding and beach conditions, strong winds and heavy rainfall" to areas including New York City and Boston on Saturday, the US National Weather Service (NWS) said. States of emergency have been declared in New York and New Jersey, both of which faced a coastal deluge in some areas. Rain and strong winds were forecast from Virginia to Maine.In Brooklyn, New York City, a man was killed by a falling tree.Figure caption, BBC Weather presenter Helen Willetts look at the impacts of the powerful Nor'easterThe man has been identified as 56-year-old Leighton Brown, an employee of the New York City Housing Authority.According to local news, he was walking through east Brooklyn neighbourhood working an extra shift when the deadly incident occurred."We mourn deeply for the loss of Leighton Brown, a NYCHA employee who faithfully served Brooklyn residents and who was known for his warm personality," the Office of the NYC Public Advocate wrote on social media.The nor'easter has caused widespread power cuts. More than 160,000 households, nearly all in the north-eastern US, have lost electricity, according to tracker PowerOutage. More than 2,400 flights were delayed and another 1,199 grounded on Saturday, according to FlightAware.A full moon was projected to worsen coastal flooding. Streets and homes were inundated with floodwater in the coastal New Jersey communities of Surf City and Manasquan on Saturday.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Surf City, New Jersey, was among coastal communities floodedNWS said in its alert: "Prepare immediately for significant inundation in low-lying areas near the shore, including roads underwater and impacts to homes and businesses." In New York, officials are warning of wind gusts of up to 55mph (86km/h) throughout the weekend, leading to downed trees and power lines."Don't travel if you don't have to," NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani told residents in a video message. "Do not drive or walk through floodwater."In the Boston area, the Red Sox moved the last game in their series against the Chicago Cubs to Sunday afternoon in Florida. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Residents on kayaks in a Beach Haven West, New Jersey, neighbourhoodA professional football match between Red Bull New York and St Louis City SC was also cancelled. The Global Citizen Festival concert in New York City's Central Park, which was to be headlined by Lauryn Hill, Wyclef Jean and John Legend, will not go ahead.Ed Sheeran's Boston concert was also among events called off due to the weather.Sheeran's concert at the Gillette Stadium in the Boston area was cancelled for safety reasons, the venue said.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Streets and homes were inundated with floodwater in coastal parts of New JerseyImage source, AFP via Getty ImagesImage caption, Waves pounded the coast in Massachusetts

schema.headline: One dead as nor'easter storm pummels New York and New Jersey

title: Indonesia Carstensz Pyramid: Papua's 'eternal snow' on Puncak Jaya is about to disappear forever
description: The treasured 'eternal snow' on this tropical island is about to disappear foreverImage source, Project Pressure/Klaus ThymannImage caption, Only smal
body: The treasured 'eternal snow' on this tropical island is about to disappear foreverImage source, Project Pressure/Klaus ThymannImage caption, Only small patches of snow remain on Papua's Sudirman RangeByAbraham UtamaBBC IndonesiaThe mountains of Papua are not far from the equator, but they've been topped with "eternal snow" for centuries.The peaks in this Indonesian region on the world's second-largest island, just north of Australia, have offered scientists countless insights into the Earth's climate history.They're also the epicentre of the spiritual universe for many Papuans - a Mecca or a Vatican, as one activist puts it.But now, nearly all the snow is gone.A century ago, the 300km (190-mile) stretch of the Sudirman Range had snow and permanent ice on all four of its major peaks.But now there are only small areas around Puncak Jaya, also known as Carstensz Pyramid, with any snow at all. These are expected to entirely disappear in a year or two.Glacier cover around the peak has shrunk from nearly 1,900 hectares (4,700 acres) in the 19th Century to about 16 hectares (40 acres) today. Almost entire glaciers have vanished within a human lifetime."There is a profound unfairness in this," says Marie Šabacká, a Czech glacier ecologist who travelled to Puncak Jaya last March in a bid to be among the last scientists to study Papua's "eternal snow".She says the tropical glaciers in Papua are unique because they are separated from other glacier systems by thousands of kilometres. Papua is home to the "last remaining tropical ice" between the Andes and Himalayas.Ice cores taken from the slopes of Puncak Jaya preserve a record of climate history. Scientists can use them to obtain information about atmospheric conditions in the region and understand changes in the planet's warmest ocean waters that surround the island - the tropical Pacific and Western Pacific Warm pool.But this archive is disappearing before scientists have had time to fully study it.Image caption, The snow cover has reduced dramatically since this photo, taken in 1936Proof of a warming planetThe retreat of Papua's glaciers is driven by the same forces affecting ice around the world, Šabacká notes, a warming atmosphere caused by human activity, including the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas.As temperatures rise, the freezing point moves higher up mountains, so more precipitation falls as rain instead of snow, even in places that once saw regular snowfall.El Niño events can accelerate this process, while local factors such as cloud cover, snowfall and mountain topography influence its pace.The mountains in Papua are just 450km (280 miles) south of the equator, where "permanent ice can survive only at very high altitudes and within a narrow range of climatic conditions", Šabacká says.A small increase in temperature, a higher freezing point or shift from snowfall to rainfall can determine whether a glacier survives at all, she adds.The glaciers' retreat is evidence the Earth has been warming over a long period - and their disappearance "removes both a biological habitat and part of a culturally significant landscape".Image source, Marie ŠabackáImage caption, Šabacká, seen taking samples from Puncak Jaya, says Papua's vanishing glaciers are unique as they are so far from other glacier systemsA spiritual anchorAt least five groups of Indigenous people have had strong spiritual ties to Puncak Jaya for generations.The Moni people refer to it as Mbainggela, and believe their ancestors watch over the mountain. To the Amungme people, the range is known as Nemangkawi, or the "White Arrow"."Parents and grandparents prayed their children would have hearts like the White Arrow, never straying from the proper path," says Elfrida Natkime, a young Amungme woman. "It symbolises honesty, purity and moral integrity."According to traditional Amungme beliefs, Nemangkawi symbolises how people should live.Amungme environmental activist Adolfina Kum stresses how important the peak is to her people - and how traditions and cultural foundations risk being shattered as the ice melts."How would Muslims feel if Mecca were destroyed? How would Catholics feel if Rome or the Vatican were destroyed?" she asks. "For the Amungme people, that is what it feels like when Nemangkawi is destroyed."Image caption, The mountain holds immense spiritual significance for Indigenous people like Justinus, a man from the Moni tribeFor many Indigenous Papuans, the disappearance of the glacier is not an isolated event.The discovery of vast copper and gold deposits transformed the region during the 20th Century, and the development of extractive industrial projects have reshaped parts of the landscape.Entire mountain faces have been excavated and roads, industrial infrastructure and settlements have transformed surrounding valleys.Papuans say the development has brought jobs, roads, education and economic opportunities, but also environmental degradation and decades of social conflict. Some have lost access to their ancestral lands as mining expanded. The BBC has approached Freeport, which operates Papua's Grasberg mine, one of the world's largest gold and copper operations, for comment."Every time I see the mountains, I feel amazed, but I also feel sadness," says Elfrida Natkime. "Since the company came, I have seen the exploitation. But the development has also provided a livelihood for many people."Image source, Project Pressure/Klaus ThymannImage caption, This 3D rendition by Klaus Thymann's Project Pressure shows ice coverage at the date of capture in 2025As local communities watch their sacred landscapes change, scientists and explorers are racing to document what is left.Using drones and three-dimensional mapping techniques, Danish researcher Klaus Thymann and his team have created a detailed model of what remains.From the early 2000s to 2025, the glaciated area has receded by 95%, he says. "There's almost no ice left. Those are the facts."Thymann says glaciers are "incredibly powerful" as indicators of climate change."When people hear that something described as 'eternal' is disappearing, it triggers a reaction," he explains.Adolfina Kum believes communities "lose an important source of strength" when sacred mountains, forests or ancestral places are disturbed."I often describe it as pulling out the roots of a tree. Once the roots are removed, the tree loses its foundation."

schema.headline: Indonesia Carstensz Pyramid: Papua's 'eternal snow' on Puncak Jaya is about to disappear forever

title: Biao Xiang: Young people in China are fangirling over a professor who gets their anxiety
description: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Young Chinese people are anxious about their future in a rapdily changing countryByFan Wang"A star sent from
body: Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Young Chinese people are anxious about their future in a rapdily changing countryByFan Wang"A star sent from the heavens," is how Zihan Han describes the man she's become a huge fan of recently, a man who young Chinese people call an "idol".Except this is no pop singer or movie star, but a 54-year old anthropologist. Professor Biao Xiang has become an unlikely guide for an increasingly disillusioned generation.And it's because of what he talks about: anxiety and how to navigate it.China's economy and tech have grown at breakneck speed, but there is plenty worrying its Gen Z, from jobs to romantic prospects to the sheer pressure of keeping up."The transition from school to the real world brings a lot of uncertainty now, and people often feel anxious because they don't know how to face it," says a 23-year-old Chinese graduate who didn't want to reveal her name because she was worried speaking to foreign media might affect her chances of finding a job back home."People need an anchor in their life. And his words make us feel there is someone that gets me."She and Zihan were among some 500 people - mostly Chinese diaspora - who piled into an auditorium recently in Singapore. Xiang spoke for more than an hour in Mandarin before he took questions. When it ended, dozens queued to meet and take photos with him. The Chinese grad called it "an academic fan meeting".Xiang has been interviewed by major Chinese outlets and has travelled to top Chinese campuses to talk, including at his alma mater, the prestigious Peking University – one talk earlier this year was live-streamed because the auditorium was full.  "When in doubt, ask Biao Xiang," has become a saying, according to Chinese media.Image caption, About 500 people heard Biao Xiang speak in Singapore recentlyIn Singapore, Xiang spoke of the recognition young people seek in today's China, where they often look to systems for approval - from competitive exams to secure jobs - and how that approval becomes a measure of self-worth, which can be exhausting and damaging. It is healthier, he suggested, to seek meaning and understanding from others and use that to understand ourselves better.These are hardly quick fixes. But in a country where discontent can be politically sensitive and heavily censored, he is a rare public figure who addresses what he calls the "pain point of the times"."Everyone knows where the issue is, but they are reluctant to look at it. Sometimes it is too painful to look at, or they don't have a way," he tells the BBC over tea in Singapore."But as an academic, it is not terrifying if you can describe it – that's how you analyse and manage it."He now lives in Germany, where he is the director of the Max Planck Institute for Social Anthropology, and studies social change in China and other parts of Asia.Xiang believes Chinese society is at a "turning point", where people are searching for meaning while making sense of rapid social and economic change. He sees contradictions – uncertain youth in a powerful, assertive country; disillusionment despite huge advancement – and his job, he says, is to unpack what is driving it.China's leader Xi Jinping has acknowledged it too: he said the "principal contradiction" was "between the people's ever-growing needs for a better life and unbalanced and inadequate development".Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Young people are seeking a new narrative in a highly competitive China, Xiang says Xiang has catchy names for what is causing this. "Floating" is how he describes people working relentlessly just to survive, like a hummingbird that keeps flapping its wings to stay mid-air."The nearby" refers to what is immediately around us. Xiang argues that people are preoccupied by the "very near" (themselves) and the very far (the world) while the space in between - "the nearby" - is neglected. This, he says, leaves them feeling disconnected.This seems to be resonating deeply with young people looking for answers. One user on RedNote writes, "He consistently views issues from the perspective of the vulnerable, attributes personal stress to macro-level causes, and encourages people to actively engage with life - it's truly wonderful."Another says, "He never spouts empty, feel-good platitudes; instead, he crouches down to face real-life dilemmas alongside us."Zihan says it boils down to Xiang's willingness to talk openly about these things: "Those who have said similar things aren't as kick-ass as Teacher Xiang, yet people who are as kick-ass as him haven't said such things."Image caption, Xiang has become famous among Chinese people for his candid lecturesBorn in 1972, Xiang came of age during another turning point, as China emerged from the brutal chaos of Mao Zedong's rule to trade with the world. It urbanised, ordinary people turned into entrepreneurs and businesses took off for the first time in the Communist nation.Growing up in Wenzhou, which transformed into an industrial port, Xiang witnessed this first-hand. "It was a vast landscape of small business owners," he recalls. "Most people didn't care too much about education, the focus was on practical matters - specifically, how to make money."And many of them did. Their children grew up in a glorious era of double-digit economic growth. But the economy slowed during Covid and hasn't bounced back. The old equation - hard work = secure job - no longer works, and they want a new narrative, Xiang says.Youth unemployment hit 21.3%, before the government stopped publishing the data in mid-2023. Those with "good jobs" - civil servants, corporate employees, engineers - are anxious about losing them.They constantly complain online about long, exhausting working hours and a toxic office culture and their fear of the "curse of 35" - a cutoff age for job advertisements, after which it is harder to find a new job.Because of censorship, it's hard to know the true extent of this mood. But that feeling of being squeezed seeps into public discourse in other ways. That anxiety quickly turns into anger in online debates, be it about university entrance exams or bride price or food safety scandals.Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Young people praying at monastery in Beijing for bright job and marriage prospects   Terms associated with this mood have been trending for years. The most famous are "lying flat", when people opt out of the rat race entirely, and "involution", a rather clunky term now commonly used to describe intense competition which generates little meaningful reward.Xiang believes two forces have amplified this anxiety - the property market and the higher education system. The property boom, fuelled by local government's reliance on land sales, tied families' sense of security and success to the values of their homes. And a rapid expansion in university enrolment raised the bar for achievement, intensifying competition.The result, he says, is a universal playbook: get a good degree, find a stable job, marry and buy a home."When 1.4 billion people are all in the same race, that is involution."About three years ago, when he learned that a camp for digital nomads where he spoke raised prices after his visit, he "realised I was no longer only known in the academic circles".Many of his peers, he said, prioritise publishing research and are "quite cold" to his methods. Some warned him about "cherishing your feathers", a Chinese expression for protecting one's reputation.But Xiang is encouraged by his popularity."If someone calls me an influencer I'll take it as a compliment. Because the real influence I can have is to make people think for themselves."

schema.headline: Biao Xiang: Young people in China are fangirling over a professor who gets their anxiety

title: News media must stay relevant or 'society will struggle', says World News Day boss
description: World News Day has grown since it began in 2018, and its message that "trusted journalism matters" aims to highlight the role of news providers in inv
body: World News Day has grown since it began in 2018, and its message that "trusted journalism matters" aims to highlight the role of news providers in investigating and explaining important events.It comes against a backdrop of what the recent Reuters Institute report described as "anxiety, disengagement, and cynicism" towards news among the public, "but also openness to new sources and formats, and continued belief in what news at its best can offer".Social media and video networks overtook news organisations' own websites and apps as the main source of online news last year, but are trusted less, the report said.In another report, published earlier this month, UK media regulator Ofcom, external also said people now get news from a wider variety of sources, with YouTube "growing rapidly" and 20% of people using AI tools to access news.But growing choice has gone hand-in-hand with greater uncertainty about who and what to believe, and traditional providers are still seen as more trustworthy, accurate and impartial than online platforms, Ofcom said.Brkic, who founded South Africa's Daily Maverick, accepts that the media landscape has changed, and said established news organisations must respond."The old days are not coming back. We need to form a new equilibrium, and the only way we can do it is that if we actually join forces," he said."If we continue like this, we're just going to be weak individual players waiting to be taken out. If we don't change something pretty fundamentally and pretty urgently, we're just going to be roadkill."Brkic said the mainstream media has "committed mistakes", but professional and reliable journalists play a vital role in society."We need to talk to our audiences and explain to them, it's not in your interest not to choose truth and trust," he said."We cannot function without a thing called the truth, without facts."The definition of "the truth" is often contested, however, as seen in US President Donald Trump's long-running battle with what he labels the "fake news media".Brkic added: "This is the information-based society. We are the infrastructure for that information-based society. And that society is actually going to really struggle without us."

schema.headline: News media must stay relevant or 'society will struggle', says World News Day boss

title: Time running out for Tennessee killer Christa Pike who says she's too damaged for death row
description: Killer Christa Pike to be executed within days - but her defence say she's a victim tooImage source, Tennesse Department of CorrectionsImage caption,
body: Killer Christa Pike to be executed within days - but her defence say she's a victim tooImage source, Tennesse Department of CorrectionsImage caption, Christa Pike's lawyers have filed a clemency petition seeking to commute her sentence ahead of the 30 September execution date ByStephanie HegartyBBC World Service correspondentAshlee Sellars last heard from her friend Christa Pike earlier this week, when Pike texted her from her cell on death row as she prepares to be killed by lethal injection by the US state of Tennessee.Pike told Sellars she did not want any of her loved ones to be present on Wednesday when she is executed. "She doesn't want us to experience that," Sellars says.Sellars finds it hard to reconcile this woman, whom she has only known to be kind and protective, with the person who committed a heinous crime 31 years ago.Pike, now 50, was 18 when she and her boyfriend at the time, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and murdered Colleen Slemmer, a 19-year-old they met at a job training camp for troubled teens.The murder created a media frenzy in Knoxville, Tennessee in 1995, when Colleen was found with a pentagram - a symbol of Satanic ritual - carved into her chest.Pike had accused Colleen of insulting her and trying to steal her boyfriend. Two other residents at the camp later testified that Pike had bragged about the murder before and after, and showed them a piece of Colleen's skull.A year later she was sentenced to death, while Shipp - who was 17 at the time - was given a life sentence with the possibility of parole. Now, after years of failed appeals, Pike's execution has been set. If it goes ahead, she will be the first woman put to death in Tennessee in more than 200 years. Only 18 women have been executed in the US since the 1970s, compared to 1,663 men.Colleen's mother has said she wants Pike's execution to happen so that her daughter "finally can be resting".Image source, Family handoutImage caption, Student Colleen Slemmer was tortured and brutally killed in the 1995 murderBut Pike's lawyers, who filed a 226-page clemency petition, are still hoping for a last-minute reprieve, while UN human rights experts have also called for the execution to be stopped., external Pike has a documented history of childhood sexual abuse, abandonment and neglect. Her lawyers believe that if she was found guilty of the same crime today as a teenager she would not receive a death sentence.In the years since her sentencing, her defence team have uncovered details about her childhood that they say the jury never had the chance to consider."It is mind-boggling that they did not present any of her history of abuse and rape, even though they knew about it," says Sandra Babcock, an expert in gender and the death penalty at Cornell Law School, who has worked on Pike's defence."Her case is so uniquely compelling, not just because of her really incomprehensible history of sexual violence but the combination of that with her youth and her mental illness."Image source, Christa PikeImage caption, Christa Pike suffered neglect and was abused by her parentsIn 1995, forensic psychologist Dr Diana McCoy was hired by Pike's defence team and found she was severely neglected by both of her parents. McCoy's report found Pike was physically and sexually abused by several of her mother's husbands and boyfriends, and raped several times, once when she was 11 and again aged 17. Later, it was discovered that she was repeatedly raped as a toddler by her grandmother's boyfriend. McCoy said Pike's mother didn't believe her that these rapes happened.But Pike's trial lawyer did not put McCoy on the stand or call many of the witnesses she recommended. These details emerged over a decade later in a court hearing reviewing her case, when a new team of lawyers claimed ineffective assistance of counsel, a claim that was denied by the judge.In 2021, Pike was diagnosed with bipolar disorder in prison and has been medicated since.Later, another forensic psychologist working for Pike's defence, Dr Bethany Brand, who assessed Pike in 2023, said her case was extremely rare because she was abused by so many people who should have protected her."Her childhood was replete with physical, sexual and emotional abuse. She was sexually violated by a number of men, starting before she was school age," she says.Brand says Pike had untreated manic episodes due to bipolar disorder and untreated PTSD. "Both of those things together absolutely influenced how threatened she felt by the girl she ended up killing and her lack of emotional control in that situation."Babcock adds: "If they let her be executed, then what it tells us is that the death penalty in this country is just a joke. It's not for the worst of the worst. It is for the people who receive the worst legal representation and who are the most damaged and vulnerable."Image source, Christa PikeImage caption, Pike, pictured as a teenager, killed Slemmer in January 1995 after telling a friend she "just felt mean that day", court documents say'She should pay for it'Last year, Tennessee's Supreme Court ruled Pike had not shown circumstances that would justify commuting her sentence. Her appeals process had been exhausted and a date was set for her execution.A federal appeals court had earlier ruled that the jury had already heard about her difficult childhood during testimony from her mother, father and aunt during her trial. And that new evidence of bipolar disorder, PTSD and brain damage "mostly repeated" what the jury had heard and would not have changed the verdict. The row has some parallels with the high-profile case of murderer Lisa Montgomery, whose lawyers also argued she was a mentally ill victim of abuse who deserved mercy.Montgomery's legal challenges failed to commute her sentence and she was executed by lethal injection in Indiana in 2021.Unless she is granted clemency by Tennessee Governor Bill Lee, Pike will be executed on 30 September. That decision is unlikely to come until the last moment and Lee has never before granted clemency in a death penalty case.The Tennessee Supreme Court this week denied Pike's request to halt the execution. Her counsel say they have been discussing next steps.On her execution day, Pike has requested an all-female team. She says being held down by a group of men will exacerbate her trauma. The state of Tennessee has said the goal is that female guards will transfer Pike to the prison where she will be executed but hasn't guaranteed it.Colleen's mother May Martinez supports Christa's execution."She did the crime. I think she should pay for it," she said on Knoxville TV station WBIR in 2021, and told the BBC this week she still stands by those comments.Pike should suffer before she dies, Martinez told WBIR. "I would feel better that she felt the same pain that Colleen did."Image source, J. Miles Carey/USA TODAY/Imagn Images via ReutersImage caption, May Martinez, mother of Colleen Slemmer, and a retired Knoxville Police department detective outside a courtroom for a post-conviction hearing in 2006"My heart breaks every single day because I keep reliving it and reliving it, and I can't no more, and I want this to happen before I die," she added."There's not a day goes by that I don't think about Colleen or how she died and how rough it was. I just want Christa down so I can end it, relieve my daughter, so she finally can be resting."The Justice Coalition, a victims' rights advocacy group, has raised money to help Martinez travel to Tennessee to watch the execution.The group's executive director, Robert Bracewell, said this sentence was determined by a jury of Pike's peers and it was what Colleen's family want."We stand firm with the family that on the 30 September her execution ought to proceed."Ashlee Sellars grapples with two seemingly conflicting beliefs: that Colleen's mother has a right to feel justice has been served and that everyone, including her friend Christa, deserves a chance at redemption."When I think about reconciling who you see on TV or the horrible tragedy that happened with Colleen, the only thing that makes sense to me is around mental health and trauma and the way that people process stuff in a moment when they don't have the things that they need," Sellars says."These horrible things happen in your youth and then those traumas moved through you, in our community, and you cause harm to somebody else."Sellars met Pike in prison while serving a 25-year sentence for her involvement in a robbery-murder. They spoke to each other through the meal flaps in their doors on the high security unit. Now, Sellars works as an advocate for justice reform and victims of crime."People want to know that everyone's life matters, right? They want to know that Colleen's life mattered," she says."Christa in this moment, I think she is fighting much more for her life to matter than she is to actually live."

schema.headline: Time running out for Tennessee killer Christa Pike who says she's too damaged for death row

title: German town bans stumbling stone memorials to Nazi victims
description: There has been a wave of criticism in Germany after the town of Heidenau, near Dresden in Saxony, decided to ban "stumbling stone" memorials to victim
body: There has been a wave of criticism in Germany after the town of Heidenau, near Dresden in Saxony, decided to ban "stumbling stone" memorials to victims of the Nazis.Germany's Education Minister Karin Prien told newspaper Bild that the ban was a "scandal".Since the 1990s, many towns in countries across Europe, including in Germany and Austria, have embedded small brass plaques in the streets in memory of Jews and other victims of Nazi atrocities.The plaques, called Stolpersteine in German, are often placed outside the houses where the victims used to live or work. They are frequently funded by donations.But now councillors from the Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party and the conservative CDU in Heidenau have voted to ban stumbling stones in their town.The AfD in Saxony has been classified as extreme-right by German intelligence, a designation the party rejects.The motion in the town council said that many citizens felt that this form of commemoration of Nazi victims was inappropriate. Memorials should in future be placed at the city's Nordfriedhof cemetery to make it "impossible to step directly onto the memorial elements", the motion stated.However, Karin Prien, a member of the CDU, criticised the decision."Anyone who banishes Stolpersteine and memorial sites commemorating Jewish life from public spaces to the cemetery is prioritising death over life and rendering Jewish people invisible once again," she told Bild.She said her own CDU party in Saxony also bore responsibility for the decision.Charlotte Knobloch, a Holocaust survivor and president of the Jewish Community in Munich, said that removing memorials from the cityscape was "completely the wrong approach".She told the Funke Media Group that she was "appalled that a democratic party would stoop to supporting such a transparent manoeuvre by the extremists of the AfD".Knobloch said that she was not a supporter of the stumbling stones, but added that "decentralised remembrance – which is not banished from public space but, on the contrary, permeates and shapes it" was crucial to a genuine culture of remembrance.In her own city of Munich, there are no Stolpersteine on municipal land. Instead, the city allows memorial plaques on public buildings.As the name suggests, Stolpersteine are intended as memorials people stumble upon, making them reflect on the history of their location.Gunter Demnig, the artist who initiated the Stolperstein project, said that given the recent electoral successes of the AfD "it was certainly to be expected that something like this would happen".The AfD recently secured major victories in state elections in Saxony-Anhalt and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern.Some branches of the populist AfD are classed as right-wing extremist by domestic intelligence, a designation the party strongly rejects.Its anti-immigration, "Germany first" and Russian-friendly agenda has found fertile ground in the country's former communist east.

schema.headline: German town bans stumbling stone memorials to Nazi victims

title: Nepal: Two bodies found after avalanche hits Himalayan base camp
description: Rescuers have recovered two bodies from the site of an avalanche that struck a climbing group camping in the Nepalese part of the Himalayas.Around a d
body: Rescuers have recovered two bodies from the site of an avalanche that struck a climbing group camping in the Nepalese part of the Himalayas.Around a dozen people are still thought to be missing after a sheet of snow fell on the base camp of Himlung Himal peak on Manang district on Sunday morning.The group of Nepalese nationals, including climbers and support staff, had been sent ahead of foreign climbers to prepare the camp and fix ropes.Forecasts showed there was heavy snowfall around the 7,126m (23,380ft) peak in recent days, which lies on Nepal's border with Tibet.Poor weather has hampered rescue efforts, with helicopters and rescue teams initially unable to reach the site.Bibhuti Chand Thakur, of Himalaya Holidays Trekking, told news agency AFP that at least eight members of his expedition team had been reported missing. The exact number of climbers still unaccounted for remains unclear.A rescue team consisting of experienced mountaineers was rushed from the Nepalese capital, Kathmandu, via helicopter. That effort is now expected to continue on Monday due to the thick snow and bad weather, local media report.The Nepalese team had been sent ahead of foreign climbers to prepare the camp, manage the route and fix ropes on the mountain.Nepal's mountain districts have seen persistent rain and snow in recent days, creating treacherous conditions for the country's economically important climbing tourism industry.Climbers were forced to leave Mount Manaslu, the eighth highest peak in the world, earlier this week due to the rising threat of avalanches.The latest death of Nepalese climbers comes less than two months after six lost their lives on Broad Peak in Pakistan, including renowned British-Nepalese mountaineer Nirmal Purja.It also comes as efforts to recover bodies continues on the Nepal-Tibet border, where more than 6,000 people are still missing after a massive flood and landslide in August.More than 1,400 people are confirmed to have died after a glacial collapse in the Himalayas sent vast quantities of water and debris careering down the Trishuli River valley, sweeping away settlements.Extreme weather events have also affected other parts of Asia in the past week.Extreme weather in the neighbouring Indian region of Uttar Pradesh has killed more than 50 people, officials there said.Meanwhile, a flood emergency disaster has been declared across Bangkok because of heavy rainfall since Thursday, with people being urged to stay at home or move to higher floors.Earlier this week, a deadly typhoon that battered Tokyo, triggering landslides in neighbouring prefectures that killed four people.Typhoon Dujuan was the latest in a series of storms in the Pacific, made more intense by the "super El Niño", an area of warmer sea water that facilitates the formation of powerful storms.

schema.headline: Nepal: Two bodies found after avalanche hits Himalayan base camp

title: Athens explosion: Six dead in blast near Acropolis in Plaka district
description: Six people have died, including a British national, in an explosion that destroyed a building containing a holiday rental property in the historic cen
body: Six people have died, including a British national, in an explosion that destroyed a building containing a holiday rental property in the historic centre of Athens.The blast on Friday happened in the Plaka area of the Greek capital, a neighbourhood close to tourist sites such as the Acropolis.Four American holidaymakers were among the dead, along with a UK national and Greek national - reportedly an elderly couple who lived in the same building. Pictures from the scene on Saturday showed emergency service workers searching through rubble, with a gas leak the suspected cause of the blast.All six bodies had been recovered by Saturday afternoon. Athens Mayor Haris Doukas said: "We are talking about an incredible disaster."The tourists were confirmed to be missing when they did not arrive for their flight at Athens airport later on Friday, news agency Reuters reported citing local police.The three-storey building completely collapsed due to the force of the blast, with neighbouring buildings damaged and debris scattered across the road.

schema.headline: Athens explosion: Six dead in blast near Acropolis in Plaka district

title: Venezuela releases dozens of political prisoners as election calls grow
description: Venezuelan authorities have released a slew of political prisoners, human rights groups say, days after the nation's interim leader met US President D
body: Venezuelan authorities have released a slew of political prisoners, human rights groups say, days after the nation's interim leader met US President Donald Trump in New York.Among those released in the early hours of Saturday morning was Wilder Vasquez, who was handed a five-year sentence in 2018 over claims he was plotting to kill former President Nicolás Maduro.Opposition figures have renewed calls for free elections after interim President Delcy Rodriguez held talks with Trump, who captured Maduro earlier this year, at the UN General Assembly on Tuesday.Her administration previously released hundreds of prisoners as part of a reconciliation effort following Maduro's seizure.However, these releases slowed to a trickle in April after Rodriguez said the scheme was "coming to an end".Venezuela's government has not made any statement concerning the latest releases, nor has it indicated whether they were the result of her conversation with the US president.Gonzalo Himiob, vice-president of rights group Foro Penal, said "a significant number" of political prisoners had been released on Saturday morning from several of Venezuela's detention centres.Venezuelan Interior Minister Diosdado Cabello, a minister closely associated with Maduro's authoritarian rule, called the interim president's meeting with Trump "a great triumph of the diplomacy of peace".But opposition voices expressed their disapproval over the meeting, viewing it as a snub of their calls – that the US has previously endorsed – for swift elections.Pedro Mario Burelli, a former Venezuelan state oil company executive and opposition commentator, called the two world leaders "the shameless puppet and her unscrupulous and undignified puppet-master", adding: "Little has changed in Venezuela under Washington's clumsy and selective oversight."Venezuela's last elections, held in 2024, in which Maduro was declared the winner, were widely disputed as rigged. Opposition tallies suggested their candidate, who stood after Machado was barred from running, had won by 70% of the vote.Despite this, the Trump administration backed Rodriguez, Maduro's former vice-president, as his successor rather than opposition leader María Corina Machado after Maduro was seized and put on trial on drug charges in January.Analysts at the time cast this decision as the US choosing short-term stability in Venezuela until elections could be held.Rodriguez used her UN General Assembly speech on Thursday to reiterate that there "will be elections in Venezuela", without specifying when.

schema.headline: Venezuela releases dozens of political prisoners as election calls grow

title: 'Scourge' of abuse must be rooted out, says Pope during Lourdes visit
description: Pope Leo has called on French bishops to root out the "scourge" of sexual abuse in the Roman Catholic church, urging them to "maintain the greatest vi
body: Pope Leo has called on French bishops to root out the "scourge" of sexual abuse in the Roman Catholic church, urging them to "maintain the greatest vigilance".The Pope delivered the message to bishops during a private meeting at the Sanctuary of Our Holy Lady of Lourdes, a holy site in southern France, on the third day of his four-day official visit to France.A 2021 inquiry found that clergy or lay members of the Church had abused about 330,000 people as children in France over 70 years.The Pope said Mass in front of thousands of worshippers in Lourdes before later meeting survivors of abuse.The Pope told the bishops: "You have faced with determination the painful scourge of abuse of minors committed by members of the clergy or within an ecclesial context."It is important to persevere along the path you have begun, maintaining the greatest vigilance."The gathering of senior church leaders was held behind closed doors and the remarks were later released to reporters.Leo then met with seven survivors of abuse by the French clergy.The Pope "thanked them for their painful testimony and reaffirmed his commitment to ensuring that the harm they experienced is not repeated for others", the Vatican said in a statement."It was extraordinary," said survivor Jean-Marie Delbos at a news conference following the encounter with the pontiff. He said Leo listened and was informed of their cases. "I never thought I would have a Pope before me," he added.The Lourdes gathering came a day after an estimated 700,000 people flocked to the Place de la Concorde in Paris to hear the pontiff speak.Huge crowds cheered and waved as he rode down the Champs-Élysées Avenue greeting followers from his open-topped popemobile.On Friday, the Pope also met French President Emmanuel Macron.During Saturday's Mass in Paris, the Pope told worshippers that Catholics should not keep their faith to themselves but "let it overflow so that those you meet may be refreshed".The leader of the Catholic Church also addressed young people in his speech, describing them as "today's Church"."How beautiful it is to see your enthusiasm, energy and commitment, and the joy you bring to Christian communities," he said.The number of regular worshippers in France has fallen from 35% of the population in 1960 to less than 5% today, while the number of priests has shrunk by two-thirds from 25,000 in 1990 to fewer than 9,000.But in recent years there have been signs of a growing interest in religious tradition, with the number of adult baptisms more than doubling in five years to hit 10,000 in 2025.Sexual abuse inside the Catholic Church has been widespread and dates back to the 1950s.The issue was first given significant media attention in the 1980s in the US and Canada before similar stories emerged across the world, including widespread historic abuse in Ireland and the UK.Reporting by the Boston Globe newspaper in the early 2000s, dramatised in the 2015 film Spotlight, exposed widespread abuse and how paedophile priests were moved around by Church leaders instead of being held accountable. It prompted people to come forward across the US and around the world.A Church-commissioned report in 2004 said more than 4,000 US Roman Catholic priests had faced sexual abuse allegations in the last 50 years, in cases involving more than 10,000 children - mostly boys.Leo's predecessor Pope Francis tried to address the issue by holding an unprecedented summit on paedophilia in the Church, and by changing its laws to explicitly criminalise sexual abuse, but problems remain.

schema.headline: 'Scourge' of abuse must be rooted out, says Pope during Lourdes visit

title: Bangkok roads submerged as flood disaster declared
description: Figure caption, Disaster declared as heavy rain sparks Bangkok floodingBySean SeddonUpdated 27 September 2026A flood emergency disaster has been decla
body: Figure caption, Disaster declared as heavy rain sparks Bangkok floodingBySean SeddonUpdated 27 September 2026A flood emergency disaster has been declared across Bangkok after more than 300mm (12in) of rain fell since Thursday, leaving roads in the Thai capital submerged. On Sunday, Bangkok's Metropolitan Authority said the rains have subsided, but canal water levels remain high. The city's governor has warned that the flooding is not yet over.People have been urged to stay at home and those living close to the city's network of canals have been advised to move their belongings to upper floors.Thunderstorms are common in Thailand at this time of year but extreme weather in recent days has inundated Bangkok's drainage system, causing traffic chaos on roads that are already famously congested. Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Canals across the Thai capital have burst their banks, leaving roads under waterSomkid Pheuk-ngam, a 67-year-old who lives near a canal just north of central Bangkok, told the AFP news agency: "The water keeps coming in. It's hard to go out now. It's like at my waist level now."I cannot go anywhere. I have been closing my shop for two days now."She said water levels in the city appeared to be worse than in 2011, when Bangkok was impacted by nationwide flooding.Hundreds were killed across Thailand then in an extreme weather event that lasted for three months. So far, no casualties have been reported in Bangkok from this latest flooding.The Thai Meteorological Service has forecast more heavy rain through the week, though the area of low pressure causing the downpours of recent days is expected to move towards central Thailand.Image source, Getty ImagesAll 50 of Bangkok's districts were declared emergency zones.On Saturday, Chadchart Sittipunt, the city's governor, said the east of the city had been hardest hit, AFP reported.He continued: "The rain keeps falling and we are doing our best. We are trying to pump the water out, but the water in canals are full... The risk areas are those who live near canals. Every canal is now filled."

schema.headline: Bangkok roads submerged as flood disaster declared

title: Iranian minister says only negotiation can end conflict after Trump rejects Hormuz deal
description: Only a "negotiated solution" can end the conflict between the US and Iran, Tehran's foreign minister has said, after President Donald Trump publicly r
body: Only a "negotiated solution" can end the conflict between the US and Iran, Tehran's foreign minister has said, after President Donald Trump publicly rejected a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.Trump told reporters at the White House that Iran's proposal was not "acceptable" and that Tehran wanted to make a deal to open the strait to commercial shipping  within seven days because "they're losing so badly".In a post on Telegram, Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi acknowledged Trump's rejection, but said Iran would wait for a "definitive" official US response.He said the president had made contradictory statements in the past.Araghchi said the conditions to open the strait were the same that had been included in a memorandum of understanding (MOU) between the US and Iran that was signed in June.Iran said it had raised reopening the strait and ending hostilities during negotiations on the sidelines of the UN General Assembly in New York this past week.The vital waterway through which around a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows has been effectively closed since the outbreak of war in February."I'm rejecting their deal," Trump said on Saturday, adding that the US already had "total control" of the strait, with "massive amounts of oil" passing through it, causing massive rises in global oil prices and steep fuel cost increases for consumers.Araghchi wrote on Telegram that Trump "has made many good statements, as well as many contradictory ones, which unfortunately we hear frequently".He continued: "We are waiting for the mediators to convey the definitive views to us, and we will make a decision based on them."Separately, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, who travelled to New York for the UN general assembly, told the BBC's US news partner CBS that "distrust created by this war needs to be overcome" in order for talks to be successful. He said the Iranians were open to talks on implementing the MOU in stages in order to end the impasse, but that the "US needs to show it does not intend to overthrow our government".Pezeshkian said Trump had "tore up" the MOU when the US resumed its bombing campaign, adding: "If we don't abide by what we have written down, can we really resolve it by dialogue?"He was also asked about Iran's new Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei, who was injured in the US strike which killed his father in February and has not been seen in public since. Reports have claimed he suffered serious injuries to his legs and face.Pezeshkian said he had met the supreme leader on two occasions, telling CBS he had "no specific ongoing health issues or challenges" and had been well enough to hold seven hours of talks.Oman, which has been acting as a mediator between the US and Iran, called for all parties to continue having open dialogue to resolve the crisis.Oman's foreign minister, Sayyid Badr bin Hamad bin Hamood Albusaidi, told the UN General Debate that "all parties" should cooperate with Oman in efforts to safeguard navigation in the strategic waterway.Trump's rejection of Iran's proposal was backed by US ambassador to Nato Matthew Whitaker.Speaking to Fox News on Saturday, Whitaker said that Iran had offered "half measures" and "illusory deals to make themselves look good on the world stage"."President Trump's right to reject it," he said.Meanwhile, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Saturday that economic sanctions imposed by the US were taking a toll on Iran.Posting on X, Bessent said Turkey, Oman and the United Arab Emirates had halted flights from various Iranian airlines, and some banks in the UAE and Turkey had stopped transactions with Iran.The Trump administration has dubbed an economic blockade on Iran "Operation Economic Outcast", with the White House attempting to use economic pressure to force Tehran to stop attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.But some economists have questioned whether the latest sanctions will be effective, as this depends on the reaction from Iran's major trading partners.These include China, the biggest buyer of Iranian oil, which has ignored previous US sanctions and continued to do business with Tehran.

schema.headline: Iranian minister says only negotiation can end conflict after Trump rejects Hormuz deal

title: Inside Yemen's front-line city as Houthis battle for control
description: Figure caption, Watch: Correspondent takes cover as approaching drone interrupts reportByNawal Al-MaghafiSenior international investigations correspon
body: Figure caption, Watch: Correspondent takes cover as approaching drone interrupts reportByNawal Al-MaghafiSenior international investigations correspondentReporting fromTaiz, Yemen"This is the first drone," said the soldier accompanying us in south-western Yemen. "It's usually followed by an attack."The buzzing sound overhead got louder as we took cover under the bushes, before climbing back into the vehicle and driving away.Within about 10 minutes, the loud thuds of strikes followed, one after another, though it was unclear where they landed.It is hard to tell where the front line begins in the mountains south-west of the city of Taiz.Saudi-backed pro-government forces are battling to push back Houthi fighters, who swept down the coast of the Red Sea earlier this month, taking control of a key shipping chokepoint and escalating Yemen's civil war. We travelled with government forces from Taiz through checkpoints to the line where their control ends and no man's land begins, in order to see the fighting up close.Homes are scattered across the slopes, but many stand abandoned after families fled to escape the fighting. It is eerily quiet, no sound of the cars or motorbikes that are continuously whizzing through the city. All you can hear is the bleating of livestock and the sound of incoming and outgoing fire."Two mortars landed here on my property," said Ali, sitting outside his home with a herd of goats, about 1km (0.6 miles) from the front line.Image source, Liam Weir/BBCImage caption, Ali has remained at home under mortar fire to look after his goatsHe told me he had sent his children to a displacement camp because they could no longer cope with the shelling and gunfire. He had stayed with his wife and sisters to look after their animals. "I am terrified," he said, "but I have no choice, we will all go hungry without our animals and die anyway."He gave only his first name, fearful of repercussions if the Houthis take over the area in the days ahead. Contacts from the Houthi side have told us they are consolidating troops, preparing for a major offensive. When we asked government forces about this they said they are aware and were preparing too.At the closest checkpoint to the front line, we met some fighters who had just returned from positions high on the mountain, just a few hundred metres from advancing Houthis. One of them said the bodies of 18 government soldiers lay in an area his unit could fire across but not reach."We shoot over them, but we can't pull them out," he said.Fighting around Taiz has intensified since the Houthis seized the strategic Red Sea port of Mokha, 85km to the west of the city, on 10 September, after a ceasefire that had largely held for four years unravelled.The group took control of a swathe of territory overlooking the strategic Bab al-Mandab Strait – a crucial shipping corridor linking Europe and Asia. This contributed to a rise in oil prices as fears rose of further disruption to supplies from the region.Taiz is Yemen's third biggest city and its cultural capital, and is home to close to a million people. It sits at a vital intersection between Houthi-controlled areas in northern Yemen and government-held ones in the south – and is hemmed in by front lines in several directions.Government forces hold the centre of Taiz, while Houthi positions lie to its north and east. The fiercest recent fighting has been on the western approaches, where the two sides are contesting high ground overlooking the city's route south. If the Houthis secure these areas, government forces could find it much harder to retake Mokha.We travelled to Taiz from Aden in the south, where Yemen's internationally recognised Presidential Leadership Council and government are based.About 30 checkpoints along the route marked stretches of road controlled by different commanders – a clear sign of the fractured make-up of the forces fighting on the government side.As we neared the city, ambulances began to pass us. We counted at least five within half an hour, heading towards Taiz's main hospital. It was clear that we were driving into a city at the heart of a brutal battle.We arrived after dark. The shops were lit, the restaurants were packed and children were playing in the streets. But every so often, other sounds broke through – the thud of shelling and the crack of gunfire from the mountains around the city.Image source, Liam Weir/BBCImage caption, An international coalition led by Saudi Arabia is providing the Yemeni government with weaponsTaiz has been a major battleground in the country's devastating civil war. After ousting the government from Sanaa in 2015, the Houthis attempted to also seize control of Taiz but were driven out of most of the city by local militiamen.Now, in their latest offensive, Houthis are making extensive use of drones alongside other weapons.Their main outside supplier is Iran, which has provided weapons, funding and military advice, according to Saudi Arabia, Western countries and UN experts. Iran, however, has previously denied supplying weapons to the Houthis and says it only supports them politically.There have been persistent reports over many years of the Houthis recruiting child soldiers, and a government soldier told us he had faced them on the front line."It's difficult to look at a Yemeni child and shoot at him. But then they are pointing the gun at you and you have to defend yourself," he said.The Houthis signed an "action plan" with the UN in 2022 pledging to end the practice. The BBC has also spoken to teenagers serving with government forces.Meanwhile a coalition led by Saudi Arabia is backing the Yemeni government, and providing it with weapons. The Saudi military has carried out hundreds of air strikes on Houthi positions on the Red Sea coast, while the Houthis have launched drones and missiles at cities and infrastructure in south-western Saudi Arabia.Image source, Liam Weir/BBC NewsImage caption, Twelve-year-old Ghana was seriously injured by a mortar while herding goatsIn the evening, at al-Thawra hospital in Taiz, casualties from the front lines were being brought into an intensive care unit where every bed we saw was occupied.Some patients were fighters, others were civilians. Twelve-year-old Ghana Nabeel had been herding goats when shrapnel struck her head. Her family said an incoming Houthi mortar had landed nearby.She lay unconscious, her head wrapped in bandages, her face swollen and bruised. Her family were waiting at her bedside to learn what life might be like if she wakes up.A doctor told me the injury had damaged her brain. "She will never be the same again," he said.Image source, Liam Weir/BBCImage caption, The UN says 130,000 people have been displaced by fighting in Yemen so far this monthAbout 20km south of Taiz, at the al-Monig displacement camp, families who had fled Mokha and villages hit by fighting were arriving, among hundreds of tents.We were told that 200 families had arrived in the previous 10 days.Maryam Saleh, not her real name, had come a week earlier from Mokha with her husband and five children. The youngest is aged seven. Maryam sat weaving a hat to sell so she could buy food for the day."We walked barefoot and we didn't carry anything with us, just our children," she told me.Her nephew was killed by shrapnel from a mortar as they fled, she said. He had been walking behind her. She described clashes and sniping both ahead of and behind the family and said she then saw armed men on the mountain."We thought we were finished," she said. The children were screaming and crying, but the family kept walking, she added.Image source, Liam Weir/BBCImage caption, Fatma Mohammed Saleh, who cannot walk, says she crawled for two days before being given a lift by a motorcyclistFatma Mohammed Saleh was lying on an empty rice sack outside another family's tent. She has a disability and cannot walk, and told me she had nowhere of her own to sleep: "I have nothing… no shelter, no mattress, no family. Nothing."Fatma said she had been with her two sons and their children when the fighting reached their village. But she was slowing them down so told them to take the children and run, she said.She spent the next two days crawling on her hands and knees, she said."I was crawling and the bullets are coming from here and the shells are there. And the bullets are here, and the shells are here. And above me it was like thunder. I was praying to God."A man on a motorbike then saw her and drove her to the camp, she said. She has not seen her family since.On 22 September, the UN refugee agency said more than 130,000 people had been displaced across Yemen so far this month, on top of 5.2 million already displaced by the civil war.It warned that another 100,000 could – like Fatma – be forced from their homes over the next three months.Additional reporting by Jasmin Dyer

schema.headline: Inside Yemen's front-line city as Houthis battle for control

title: Tukaram Mundhe: Why some Indian civil servants become heroes for doing their jobs
description: Among the thousands of civil servants who keep India's vast government machinery running, a small number become unlikely public figures every few year
body: Among the thousands of civil servants who keep India's vast government machinery running, a small number become unlikely public figures every few years.Tukaram Mundhe, 51, is one of them.The commissioner of Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration, he has led a series of enforcement drives since taking charge in May. His teams have inspected restaurants and other food businesses, uncovering pest infestations, poor hygiene and expired food.He has also highlighted large gaps between what hospitals pay for common medical supplies and what patients are charged.These actions have made Mundhe a social-media celebrity, with videos and images from inspections widely shared online. Hundreds of people have commented that they wished officers like him could be sent to fix food safety concerns in their state. Mundhe is not alone. In Gurugram, a suburb of Delhi, district town planner RS Batth has won praise for acting against illegal construction and encroachments.But why are these officials treated like heroes for doing their jobs?In India, civil servants are responsible for many services people rely on every day, from issuing documents to policing, food safety and healthcare. But many are also accused of delays, bribes and making people run from pillar to post.So when an official appears to cut through the red tape, the response can be surprisingly enthusiastic."What should have been normal has become exceptional," says retired civil servant Kamal Kant Jaswal.For many citizens, delays, bureaucratic hurdles and indifferent treatment have become so familiar that efficient governance now stands out as an exception, he adds. Mundhe is not the first official to gain recognition for doing exactly that. One of the most prominent examples is TN Seshan, who became a household name as India's chief election commissioner in the 1990s for fearlessly enforcing rules.Kiran Bedi, the first woman to join the officer ranks of the Indian Police Service, was nicknamed "Crane Bedi" in the early 1980s after it was widely reported that she got an illegally parked car belonging to then prime minister Indira Gandhi towed away (it was removed by a sub-inspector who reported to her, who said years later that she supported, external his decision). Ashok Khemka became nationally known after intervening in a controversial land transaction in 2012, while police officer Neeraj Jadaun was praised for confronting a mob during deadly religious violence in Delhi in 2020. These stories have made the idea of the "honest" or "no-nonsense" bureaucrat both familiar and rare. Jaswal, however, points out that thousands of officials in India do their jobs without attracting public attention."Their work may not involve much direct contact with citizens, or may simply be less visible."For ordinary people, however, a visit to a government office is often seen as an exhausting process.Rajesh Singh, 43, who works at a finance company in Delhi, says he has experienced long waits to get his work done and even longer processes to solve complaints."What is supposed to take 24 hours, I have personally experienced being stretched to six months with no guarantee of a positive outcome even then," he says.But an officer praised for enforcing rules can also face criticism for applying them too rigidly without taking into account ground realities.Mundhe has been criticised by sections of the food and hospitality industry over his enforcement drives. He has rejected allegations of selective or unlawful action, saying inspections are evidence-driven and licences are suspended only in serious cases.Batth, too, has faced flak for acting against illegal encroachments, with critics alleging his enforcement is selective and disproportionately affects vulnerable people. In several viral videos, he has said his actions are carried out strictly under town-planning rules.Jaswal explains a street vendor's stall may be an unauthorised structure in the eyes of the law, but could be a family's only source of income. And in a country where millions migrate to cities in search of work, unsanctioned living spaces could be the only way to find a place to stay.This tension between the law and economics helps explain why the same enforcement action can be viewed as both lawful and harsh.Bureaucrats also face challenges of their own while carrying out their duties.Pushpa Sundar, who briefly served as a civil servant and has written extensively on development issues, says officers can face political pressure and transfers when they refuse to comply with demands."They too have families, careers and financial responsibilities and it needs extraordinary courage to risk those things in order to act independently," she says.She argues that officers need stronger institutional support when they refuse to do something illegal or improper.Jaswal remembers facing such pressure himself.In 1974, when he was district magistrate of Uttarkashi in what was then undivided Uttar Pradesh, a senior minister was contesting the state legislature election.He says he had to turn down a number of demands from the minister as they were against the rules. The minister won the election and Jaswal says he got his "marching orders soon after".But when he left for his next assignment, people stood in the summer heat for several kilometres on his way to say goodbye.The relationship between politicians and civil servants, he says, is rarely straightforward. Many civil servants who seek desirable postings or rely on political support choose the path of least resistance, while standing up to political pressure entails certain costs, he says. Social media has also changed how quickly an officer can become a public sensation.An action once limited to a district can now be filmed, shared and viewed by millions within hours."Social media can turn an official into a national talking point almost overnight," Sundar says.That is partly what happened with Mundhe, whose inspection videos have turned routine enforcement into a widely watched spectacle.Mundhe, however, sees it differently.Speaking to the BBC last month, he said his actions were driven by public-health concerns and that businesses complying with rules had nothing to fear.For Mundhe, the attention is beside the point. The rules already exist and his job is simply to enforce them.But the public fascination is about more than just one officer.When basic government functions are carried out visibly and consistently, they can seem extraordinary - particularly because so many people have come to expect otherwise.

schema.headline: Tukaram Mundhe: Why some Indian civil servants become heroes for doing their jobs
